docs.title: Erosion brand kit
docs.text: The Erosion mark is a rounded phone cut into an E. Three rows of diagonal cuts step left as they descend. Fired-clay slats and split copper tips follow the phone’s right edge, and a single centered camera slot finishes the top.

docs.title: Download the artwork
docs.text:
Asset Use Primary logo · SVG · transparent PNG Light slides, articles, and print layouts Reverse logo · SVG · transparent PNG Dark slides and photography with a dark, quiet area One-color logo · SVG Single-ink printing and monochrome layouts Editable PowerPoint mark Ten individually editable vector shapes Standalone mark · SVG · 512 px PNG Icons, avatars, and small placements Social card · 1200 × 630 PNG · editable SVG Link previews, announcements, and presentation covers CSS color tokens Website and digital campaign styling

Use the full logo at 120 px wide or larger. Below that, use the standalone mark down to 16 px. Leave at least the height of one shelf of the E clear on every side. The logo SVGs contain paths so they scale and print without installing a font.

docs.title: Marketing materials
docs.text:
Set headlines in a bold sans serif such as Inter, with Georgia Italic for short emphasis. Use a monospace face for Rust and technical labels. Keep body copy in Basalt on Chalk. The reverse treatment uses Chalk text and Copper accents on Basalt.

The soil-layer backdrop uses the colored bands from the social card. On the homepage, the sample screenshots sit in front of those layers.

The Rust gear beside the headline is the unmodified logo from the Rust project’s artwork collection, used under CC BY 4.0.

docs.title: Using device capabilities from Rust
docs.text: Controls Gallery → Device utilities exercises clipboard, Keychain/Keystore, authentication and haptics with disposable sample data. Erosion delivers pending capability results to the app across page changes.

docs.title: Enable capabilities in a framework sample
docs.text:
Use a small .xcconfig under ios/config named for the capitalized Android Gradle module (for example, gallery → Gallery.xcconfig). The Gradle build reads the same simple NAME = value declarations as Xcode. Set the iOS target's Debug and Release config files to this file, apply the DeviceCapabilities XcodeGen template and expose MRustCapabilities and the applicable usage-description settings in the target Info properties, as in Gallery and Field Catch. The standalone counter has its own Gradle and XcodeGen projects. When adding a capability there, use the sample manifest, usage descriptions, and platform dependencies for that feature as a reference. Once the host supports it, another Rust screen in the same app can use it too.

Setting Meaning MRUST_CAPABILITIES Space-separated entries from files photos camera share audio location maps secure biometrics clipboard haptic rtc tilt. An absent declaration enables none. MRUST_CAMERA_USAGE, MRUST_MIC_USAGE, MRUST_LOCATION_USAGE, MRUST_FACE_USAGE User-facing purpose strings. Use the Face ID string for protected secrets as well as standalone authentication. MRUST_MAP_STYLE MapLibre style filename in the app assets or an HTTPS style URL. The MapLibre build loads worldwide vector tiles and labels from OpenFreeMap as the camera moves. Uncached regions need internet access. The bundled offline map covers central San Francisco with 4,827 active street segments from San Francisco Public Works. Street geometry is distributed under the Open Data Commons Public Domain Dedication and License. DataSF source. Supply licensed tiles and attribution for a production basemap.

Gradle merges permissions for enabled capabilities and installs a private FileProvider for the camera and share sheet. Android map-enabled samples use MapLibre by default. Field Catch can select Google Maps at build time when the build machine has a key in ~/.config/erosion/android_map_key.txt. iOS uses system MapKit. A map of saved pins works with location access denied. Device permission prompts occur when the user invokes the feature.

docs.title: Issue requests
docs.text:
Keep an increasing request ID in the app model. Push an Effect::Capability { id, request } into the app's effects queue and handle HostEvent::CapabilityResult { id, outcome } in DeclarativeApp::on_host_event. Compare the ID with the operation you are expecting. Store the ID with its owning model data until completion or abandonment. Cancel with Effect::CancelCapability { id }. Camera, picker, and share UI can move the app out of the foreground while an operation is pending.

Task Rust request or control Capture or choose a photo Operation::CapturePhoto, Operation::PickPhoto; display the returned asset with asset.image("Photo").key("preview"). Import, export, share Operation::ImportDocument, Operation::Export { asset }, Operation::Share { text, assets }. Android reports Presented when it opens the chooser. UIKit reports completion or cancellation when the sheet closes. Record a memo Operation::Record emits Recording. Issue StopRecording or DiscardRecording with its own ID. The original request receives the final asset or cancellation. Play a memo Operation::PlayAudio { asset }, PauseAudio, ResumeAudio, SeekAudio { millis }. The original play request receives progress with position and duration in milliseconds, then a terminal result. Cancel it to release the player. Get location Operation::Locate { watch: false } returns one Fix. With watch: true it emits fixes until canceled or backgrounded. Each includes coordinates, timestamp, accuracy in meters, and reduced-accuracy status. Display a map map("field", Map { center, zoom: 13.0, recenter: 0, pins, overlays }) takes its map data from erosion_ui::map. Give the control a height or a flexible parent. Keep pin IDs stable and increment recenter to move the camera explicitly. Bind .on_map_idle(...) for center and zoom or .on_map_heading(...) to follow rotation. A selected pin produces HostEvent::Pick. Open directions Operation::Directions { point } opens the platform maps handler. Android tries a navigation intent, then a maps directions URL. Check access Operation::Permission { feature: Permission::Microphone }; Camera and Location are also supported. Operation::OpenSettings opens the app's OS settings. Android's external camera path checks hardware availability and uses a temporary URI grant. Store a small secret Operation::SecretSet { key, value, protected: true }, SecretGet { key }, SecretDelete { key }. Read returns Outcome::Text. A protected read requires the OS to authorize the key operation. Use protected: false for an ordinary app-private secret. Verify identity Gallery uses Operation::VerifyDeviceOwner for a system biometric or screen-lock prompt (screen lock on Android 9). A device without a secure screen lock reports SetupRequired. Operation::Authenticate requests biometrics specifically. Protected storage independently enforces read access. Clipboard and haptics ClipboardWrite { text }, ClipboardRead, Haptic { feedback: Feedback::Selection }. Trigger clipboard reads from an explicit paste action. Haptics also accept Success, Warning, and Firm. Gallery uses Firm for one stronger tap.

AssetRef contains a private identifier, display name and MIME type. Persist it alongside the note. Bytes remain in the app container. The file adapters stage writes, move completed files into place, and clean abandoned staging files on a fresh process. An in-process Android Activity recreation can resume a pending file picker. An interrupted capture after process death can be retried. Shares give the recipient temporary read access. The imported files and notebook are local to this app installation.

docs.title: Verification
docs.text: Use the commands in the repository’s sample guide (samples/README.md). Exercise clipboard and storage round trips in Controls Gallery. Check tactile feedback and device authentication on a physical phone.

docs.title: Field Catch EULA and player terms
docs.text:
Effective November 27, 2026

Walk to play. Stop moving before looking at the map or through the camera. Play in daylight or good visibility, on level ground in an open area where you have permission to be.

docs.title: Skip any unsafe catch
docs.text: A virtual ball can land across a road, near water, on private property, or beyond a fence. GPS can be wrong. Check your surroundings yourself. Never cross traffic, climb, trespass, or run to beat the timer. Tap “Skip unsafe catch” to retry the turn. Both players keep their scores.

docs.title: Playing with someone else
docs.text: Share the field code with someone you trust. During play your partner can receive your location. Unmute your microphone or share a camera view only when you want your partner to hear or see you. Respect other people’s privacy and get permission before showing them on camera.

docs.title: Agreement to play
docs.text: These terms are between you and Faisal Waris, the developer of Field Catch. By choosing “I agree,” you agree to these rules and acknowledge that moving outdoors can involve falls, collisions, or other injuries. You can leave the field at any time. These terms preserve your rights under applicable law, including rights relating to personal injury.

docs.title: App license
docs.text:
For copies obtained from Apple’s App Store, Apple’s Standard Licensed Application End User License Agreement governs use of the software. These player terms supplement that license. For the Android app, the developer grants you a personal, nonexclusive license to install and play Field Catch on a device you own or control. Open-source components remain available under their respective licenses.

Read Apple’s standard EULA · Field Catch privacy policy · Contact the developer

docs.title: Field Catch Privacy Policy
docs.text:
Effective November 27, 2026 · Field Catch for iPhone and iPad

Field Catch lets two people play together without giving us a name, email address, or phone number. We don’t keep a history of your matches, record your calls, sell personal information, or use advertising or analytics trackers.

docs.title: When you create or join a field
docs.text:
Field Catch uses Google Firebase to introduce your device to your partner’s. Firebase assigns an anonymous player identifier. Its Realtime Database stores the field code, the two players’ identifiers, the field’s expiration time, and the technical messages the devices exchange to find each other. These messages can include network addresses. Your device also contacts Google’s STUN service to find its public network address. A direct connection can reveal that address to your partner.

A field expires after about an hour. This ends player access to its signaling records. The records can remain in Firebase until the developer removes them. Firebase also processes technical information such as IP addresses to operate and secure its services. Google describes its retention periods in its Firebase privacy information.

docs.title: What your partner receives
docs.text:
During a match, game updates travel directly between the two devices over an encrypted WebRTC connection. When you tap Ready to catch and allow location access, your phone shares precise position readings with your partner so both phones can place the ball and score the catch.

Your microphone starts muted. Unmuting shares your voice with your partner. A video call uses the camera with your permission. View in AR uses the rear camera on your device. Share AR lets your partner see that view. Firebase does not receive your gameplay location readings, scores, microphone audio, or camera stream.

docs.title: Maps, storage, and your choices
docs.text:
Field Catch uses Apple Maps to display the playing field. Loading the map can send requests to Apple for the area shown. The app remembers the last map center and zoom on your device. Versions that ask you to agree before playing also store the accepted terms version locally. Field Catch EULA and player terms Apple’s privacy policy

You can mute the microphone, stop sharing AR, end a call, or leave the field. Leaving closes the peer connection. You can revoke location, camera, or microphone access at any time in your device’s Settings → Privacy & Security. Deleting the app removes its local settings.

docs.title: Contact
docs.text: For a privacy question or a request about a Firebase field record, contact Faisal Waris through the Field Catch website’s issue tracker. That page is public. Please describe your request in general terms and keep field codes, locations, and other personal details out of the post.

docs.title: Contact the developer
docs.text:
Email Faisal Waris at ffsvoice@gmail.com for help with Field Catch. If something went wrong during a match, include your phone model, operating system version, and the last thing you tapped.

You can also report a bug or request a feature on GitHub. GitHub reports are public. Keep field codes, precise locations, and personal information out of your report.

docs.title: My partner is stuck on Connecting
docs.text: Check that both phones have internet access. Leave the field on both phones, then have one player tap Create a Field and share the new code privately. The other player should tap Join a Field and enter that code. If it still hangs, try another network and tell us which phone created the field and which one tried to join.

docs.title: The app doesn’t register my catch
docs.text: Tap Ready to catch and allow precise location while playing. After the ball lands, Field Catch needs two accurate GPS readings within 12 metres of the flag. Check the GPS precision shown on the map. If the flag is across a road or anywhere unsafe, tap Skip unsafe catch. Both players keep their points.

docs.title: My partner can’t hear me
docs.text:
Each player starts muted. On the phone sending the audio, tap the microphone to unmute. On iPhone, open Settings → Privacy & Security → Microphone and check that Field Catch has access. On the receiving phone, check the volume and whether audio is playing through connected headphones.

Privacy policy · Player terms

docs.title: Create a standalone app
docs.text:
Your first app is a counter with one button. You can run its Rust test as soon as you have Git and Rust installed. To see the button on a phone, you’ll also need the tools for that platform.

Run the commands below from the directory where you keep your projects. The first command installs the generator at a specific framework revision. The second creates a Git repository named hello-mobile. Choose your own identifier if you intend to distribute the app. Erosion uses it for both the Android application ID and the iOS bundle identifier.

cargo install --git https://github.com/fwaris/erosion.git --rev aaba3e2591f56f5f36da9349f3373a355e528282 --locked cargo-erosion
cargo erosion new hello-mobile --id com.example.hellomobile --name "Hello Mobile"
cd hello-mobile
cargo test --locked

With an Android device connected, run ./scripts/run-android.ps1 in PowerShell on Windows. With an iPhone simulator booted, run bash scripts/run-ios.sh on your Mac. Tap Increment and the count changes from 0 to 1.

Open src/lib.rs to change the counter. Add a variant to Msg, handle it in update, and bind a control to it in view. The generated AGENTS.md describes this pattern for contributors and coding agents. Share the repository with its lockfile. Teammates can use its local scripts directly. Screens and state

docs.title: What lives in the new repository?
docs.text: Edit src/lib.rs for behavior, android/app for the Android manifest and resources, and ios/project.yml for the iOS target and signing settings. The generated scripts use cargo metadata --locked to locate the framework checkout that matches your lockfile. That checkout supplies the shared build helpers, Rust bridge, and native renderers. A teammate can clone your app and run either script with the platform tools installed.

docs.title: Platform setup
docs.text:
Android on Windows. Install PowerShell 7 and JDK 21. In the Android SDK Manager, install SDK Platform 35, Build Tools 36.0.0, and NDK r27d. If you also want to build the Field Catch sample, install SDK Platform 36. Add the Rust targets for an ARM phone and an x86-64 emulator:

rustup target add aarch64-linux-android x86_64-linux-android

iOS on an Apple Silicon Mac. Install Xcode, an iOS simulator runtime, and XcodeGen. Add the two Rust targets below. The launcher uses XcodeGen to turn the app’s ios/project.yml into an Xcode project and uses Xcode to build and install the app.

rustup target add aarch64-apple-ios aarch64-apple-ios-sim

docs.title: Run one sample
docs.text:
To explore the three framework examples, clone the Erosion repository and run these commands from its root. Each command builds, installs, and opens the selected application.

Sample Android on Windows (PowerShell 7) iOS on a Mac (Bash) Controls Gallery ./scripts/run-android.ps1 gallery bash scripts/run-ios.sh gallery Falling Blocks ./scripts/run-android.ps1 falling-blocks bash scripts/run-ios.sh falling-blocks Field Catch ./scripts/run-android.ps1 field-catch bash scripts/run-ios.sh field-catch

Android. Start an emulator or connect a phone with USB or wireless debugging enabled. With multiple devices connected, use adb devices -l and append -Serial <serial>.

iOS. Start an iPhone simulator, or pass its UDID to boot it, for example bash scripts/run-ios.sh gallery "$SIMULATOR_UDID". List simulators with xcrun simctl list devices available. For a paired physical iPhone, set DEVELOPMENT_TEAM to your Apple team ID and run bash scripts/run-ios.sh gallery --device "$IPHONE_UDID" with the phone unlocked. Find the device with xcrun devicectl list devices.

Field Catch multiplayer. Field Catch uses Firebase when the build account has ~/.config/erosion/field-catch-firebase.json. For local play, start cargo run --locked -p field-catch-broker in a separate terminal. Android forwards port 8787 automatically in local mode. An iOS simulator can use the broker on its Mac. For a physical iPhone or players on separate computers, follow the Field Catch network setup in the repository’s sample guide.

docs.title: Upgrade a generated app
docs.text:
1. In the app's Cargo.toml, set both Erosion Git dependencies to the same new commit. Run cargo update -p erosion-ui -p erosion-native-host and commit Cargo.lock. Preserve the Rust package name, Android application ID, iOS bundle ID, and app data keys so the installed app upgrades in place.
  2. Replace study.mobile.StudyActivity with dev.erosion.host.ErosionActivity in the Android manifest and in the component launched by scripts/run-android.ps1. Keep the existing rust.app metadata. For custom JNI callers, the bridge class is dev.erosion.host.ErosionBridge and its shared library is liberosion.so.
  3. In the XcodeGen project, replace the individual framework Swift source entries with one source directory, generated/framework/ios/Host. Set the bridging header to generated/framework/native-host/ErosionBridge.h. Keep the existing RustApp value and scene declaration. Custom C callers now use erosion_exchange and erosion_release.
  4. Change Rust imports and matches from erosion_ui::Event to erosion_ui::HostEvent. Existing Application implementations and native factories continue to work. A single-screen counter can replace its adapter and export with erosion_ui::erosion_app!(Model::default, update, view); and remove the old adapter imports. Apps with lifecycle hooks can implement erosion_ui::app::DeclarativeApp and return an AppAdapter from their factory.
  5. Remove the numeric first argument from strata_screen and widgets::screen. For a page stack, replace the old route and presentation hooks with fn navigation(&self) -> Navigation { self.nav.navigation() }. Render self.nav.current() and use push_with_transition for an explicit transition. Store pending request IDs in the model and decide which operations continue when a page closes.
  6. For low-level controls, wrap canvas and map data in Control::Canvas(canvas::Canvas { ... }) and Control::Map(map::Map { ... }). Move glyphs onto MapPin and circles into Map::overlays. Field Catch owns its AR scene payload and supplies its renderer through Control::NativeSurface. Set button icons on the button builder. Direct node readers can use key(), control(), and style().
  7. Run cargo test --locked, then run the app's Android and iOS scripts. Install over the existing app and check a previously saved setting on both platforms.

docs.title: Navigation and effects
docs.text: Imagine editing a task on a phone. You expect Back to return you to the same filtered list. You might also expect Back to throw away the title you just typed. Both behaviors come from where the app stores those two values. The Projects exhibit lets you try them side by side. In Live monitor, leaving the screen also stops a worker that has been sending it fresh prices.

docs.title: Push and pop a page
docs.text:
Gallery keeps its search text in the app model and its page stack in Routes<Page>. Search for “slider,” open the matching exhibit, then go back. The catalog still shows the same search because both pages use the same app instance.

To add a destination, give it a variant in your app’s Page enum. A button can bind to Msg::Open(Page::Detail). Handle that message in DeclarativeApp::update by calling self.nav.push(page). In view, match on self.nav.current() to choose the content. The navigation hook passes the stack to Erosion:

fn navigation(&self) -> Navigation {
    self.nav.navigation()
}

Handle system Back in on_host_event with self.nav.pop(). Use present(page) for a sheet or push_with_transition(page, Transition::Fade) for a fade. Field Catch also calls handle_root_back() on the returned navigation value so it can leave AR or end a session from the root page.

Erosion gives each visit its own internal ID. If a late tap arrives from the first visit to Detail after a second visit has opened, the runtime discards it. The app just works with Page::Detail. A device reply has a different lifetime: a save that belongs to a document may still matter after the editor closes.

docs.title: Give each section its own model
docs.text:
Open Controls Gallery → Projects. Filter the list to “garden” and open the first project. Its editor starts with a copy of the saved task. Back drops the draft. Save copies the edited title into the Gallery’s records before popping the editor. Back from the detail page reveals the original filter. Leave Projects entirely and the next visit starts with an empty filter.

The application still has one root model. Its route stack owns just the pages the user has opened. A page can carry ordinary Rust values. For example:

enum ProjectsPage {
    List { filter: String },
    Detail(usize),
    Editor { project: usize, draft: String },
}

At the moment the editor opens, three pages are on the Projects stack. Here’s what each one owns and when the user will see that value again.

Value Where Gallery keeps it What happens on Back “garden” in the filter field The list page Opening a project covers the list. Returning to it reveals the same filter. Leaving Projects drops it. The title being typed The editor page Closing the editor drops its draft. Opening another editor makes a fresh copy of the saved title. The saved task title The Gallery’s project records Save updates the record before popping the editor. The detail page then renders the new title. It lasts for this app session.

A large app can follow the same pattern one section at a time. Borrow the active page with nav.current() to render it and nav.current_mut() to edit it. Popping a page drops the Rust values it owns. Falling Blocks allocates its board when the player starts a game. Its Play page owns the board through a Box, so returning to the lobby releases the board while the app keeps the high score. To keep a value through process exit, save it separately. Falling Blocks writes the high score to a file.

Projects also has its own messages. In samples/gallery/src/projects.rs, the editor binds the Save button to the section’s Msg::Save. The Gallery wraps the whole screen with .map_msg(Msg::Projects). A tap then reaches the Gallery as a Projects message, and the Gallery passes it to the section’s update function. This lets someone editing the task feature find its fields, buttons, and rules together.

docs.title: Receive messages from background work
docs.text:
Open Controls Gallery → Live monitor and leave the phone untouched. Once a second, a Rust worker generates prices for three fictional stocks. When a batch arrives, the prices and the received-batch count change together. This example runs offline.

A button press already arrives on the phone’s UI thread. The quote worker runs on another thread, and the phone may be idle when its next batch is ready. Erosion supplies an AppSender<Self::Msg> in the app’s on_attach hook. The app gives the worker a clone. Sending a message wakes the native UI loop, which delivers the message to the same update method that handles the Pause button. The worker can finish its job without touching a native control or locking the dashboard model.

Here’s the sending end from samples/gallery/src/monitor.rs. It runs inside the worker’s loop:

match sender.try_send(Msg::QuoteBatch(run, quotes)) {
    Ok(()) | Err(TrySendError::Full(_)) => {}
    Err(TrySendError::Closed(_)) => break,
}

A successful send puts the batch in a bounded queue. If the queue fills, the monitor skips that batch because another price will arrive shortly. An app sending an edit that must be saved would need a different policy. Both error variants return the original message so the producer can keep it. A closed sender means its host attachment has ended and this worker can exit. The example uses a standard Rust thread. An app that already uses Tokio can give the same sender to one of its tasks.

docs.title: Pause, leave, and come back
docs.text:
Tap Pause feed. The prices stay on screen because the route still owns the dashboard model. The app drops a separate cancellation handle, which wakes the worker and ends its loop. Resume starts another worker from the displayed prices. Putting the app in the background also stops the feed. On returning, a paused dashboard stays paused. Back closes the route altogether, so the next visit starts at zero batches.

There’s a small race worth testing in your own app. A worker could queue one last batch just before the user taps Pause. By the time the phone delivers it, the user may already have tapped Resume. Live monitor gives each run an ID and checks it in Dashboard::receive. Only a batch from the current run can change the displayed prices. If the native host is recreated, Erosion closes the old sender before calling on_detach. The next on_attach supplies a fresh sender.

docs.title: Request a native operation
docs.text:
The app queues effects and drains them in effects(). Assign a fresh request ID for each operation and store it with the domain data that will receive the result. A save can update an item while its editor is closed. Reopening the editor renders the saved value. If leaving should abandon an operation, clear the pending request in update and issue Effect::CancelCapability { id } to stop the native work.

use erosion_ui::{capabilities::Operation, runtime::Effect};
let request = Effect::Capability { id: 42, request: Operation::PickPhoto };

On HostEvent::CapabilityResult, match the ID before applying the outcome. An Outcome::Asset contains a private asset reference that can be persisted with the note. Handle cancellations and permission denial explicitly. The device guide lists operations and sample setup.

docs.title: Deep links and local notifications
docs.text: An app can assign a stable note ID when saving and open links such as mrust-notes://note/2. Schedule a local notification with Effect::ScheduleReminder { id, title, url, delay_seconds }. Handle HostEvent::OpenUrl { url } in Rust so tapping the reminder routes to the same saved note as opening the link. Register the URL scheme when packaging a new app. Android may defer delivery when exact alarms are unavailable.

docs.title: Sample applications
docs.text:
Build and launch the samples from the workspace. Each sample has a Rust crate, an Android application ID, and an Xcode scheme.

Sample Rust crate directory Android application ID iOS scheme Controls Gallery samples/gallery study.samples.gallery Gallery Falling Blocks samples/falling-blocks study.samples.blocks FallingBlocks Field Catch samples/field-catch com.erosion.fieldcatch FieldCatch

docs.title: Controls Gallery
docs.text:
Layout Inputs & form state Keyed collections Motion & navigation Drawing surface Video surface Device utilities

Open Inputs to exercise native editing, switches, sliders, and date selection. Search by control name, such as slider, canvas, or clipboard. Layout demonstrates rows, columns, wrapping, overlays and adaptive panels. Device utilities gives clipboard, haptics, authentication and secure storage their own instructions and results.

docs.title: Two exhibits to try when your app grows
docs.text:
Open Projects, type “garden” in the filter, and select Community garden. Choose Edit task, change the title, and go back without saving. The detail screen shows the original task. Try again and choose Save. This time the detail screen shows your edit, and going back once more brings you to the filtered list. The filter, the draft, and the saved record each live as long as the part of the app that owns them. How Projects divides its state

Open Live monitor and put the phone down for a few seconds. The batch count increases as a worker sends new simulated quotes. Tap Pause feed and switch to another app. When you return, the display is still paused at the same prices. Tap Resume feed to continue, or go back to the catalog and reopen the exhibit to start over. How a worker wakes the screen

docs.title: Falling Blocks
docs.text:
Start the game, move or rotate the piece, and drop it. The Rust model owns timing, board state, and collision detection. The drawing surface receives the updated board. Pause and return to the game to exercise lifecycle behavior.

Model, message, and update explains how the buttons and swipes reach the same game rules.

docs.title: Field Catch
docs.text:
Two players share a field code and take turns kicking and catching over six turns. Before the partner joins, the creator chooses a maximum kick distance of 30, 60, or 100 metres and wind from calm to strong. Selecting 100 metres shows a warning about the distance.

Aim a kick Track the flight Reach the landing flag Choose field conditions Play with a partner Learn the rules

The kicker drags the puck to set direction and power, then taps KICK. The guide stays aligned with the target when the map rotates. During flight, the map reports the ball’s height and distance from the catcher. At touchdown, the catcher has 60 seconds to reach the flag. Two consecutive accurate GPS readings within 12 metres register the catch. A catch earns one point. During the first 30 seconds after touchdown, it also earns a bonus that starts at five points and drops by one every six seconds.

The catcher can switch to View in AR and share the rear-camera view with the kicker. Players can also unmute their microphones or invite each other to a video call. The match continues while they talk. Field Catch owns the scoring, peer messages, and choice of camera view. Erosion delivers the GPS fixes and maps touch input to the game’s messages. Explore the Rust update loop.

docs.title: Run regression checks
docs.text:
cargo test --workspace --release --locked -- --test-threads=1

On a dedicated Android test installation run ./scripts/test-samples-android.ps1 -Serial <serial>. On the Mac run bash scripts/test-samples-ios.sh "$SIMULATOR_UDID". The native tests create sample data. Physical camera capture, microphone quality, biometric success, and haptic feedback still need phone sign-off.

docs.title: Screens and state
docs.text: Open src/lib.rs in a generated app. Everything you need to change the counter is in that file, including its test. The same Rust view runs on both phones. Erosion creates the native buttons and labels and keeps them in sync with the model.

docs.title: Model, message, and update
docs.text:
Follow Increment through the starter. The button binds a press to Msg::Increment. The app decides what that message does in update. When view reads the new count, Erosion compares the screen with the previous one and sends the changed label to the host.

use erosion_ui::{
    declarative::{button, strata_screen, text, ViewScreen},
    design::Role,
    erosion_app,
    view,
};

#[derive(Default)]
struct Model {
    count: u64,
}

#[derive(Clone)]
enum Msg {
    Increment,
}

fn update(model: &Model, msg: Msg) -> Model {
    match msg {
        Msg::Increment => Model {
            count: model.count.saturating_add(1),
        },
    }
}

fn view(model: &Model) -> ViewScreen<Msg> {
    view! {
        strata_screen(include_str!("../app-name.txt")) {
            text("count", format!("Count: {}", model.count), Role::Title);
            button("increment", "Increment").on_press(Msg::Increment);
        }
    }
}

erosion_app!(Model::default, update, view);

#[cfg(test)]
mod tests {
    use super::*;
    #[test]
    fn increment_updates_count() {
        let model = update(&Model::default(), Msg::Increment);
        assert_eq!(model.count, 1);
    }
}

docs.title: Where messages come from
docs.text:
For the counter, every change begins with a tap. Other screens can change while the user’s hands are off the phone. Gallery also needs to know when the OS finishes a clipboard request and when the user presses Back. It implements DeclarativeApp and registers an AppAdapter::new(app) in its native factory. The adapter keeps a MountedView for that app instance and dispatches each input once.

Input Where it goes A press on a button with .on_press(Msg::Save) The adapter resolves the binding and calls the app’s update(Msg::Save). A quote from Live monitor’s worker The worker queues a typed message through AppSender. Erosion wakes the UI loop and calls the app’s update method. System Back or a clipboard result The app’s on_host_event receives the unbound HostEvent. The app can pop a page or match a result to a pending request.

To follow a message that starts outside the UI, open the Live monitor walkthrough. It covers what happens when a worker finishes after the user has left the screen.

An app can also supply a snapshot, request clock ticks, or keep the screen awake during a match. These hooks have defaults, so a new feature only needs the ones it uses. The underlying runtime::Application trait is available if you want to implement dispatch and rendering yourself.

Gallery uses toggle(...).on_toggle(Msg::Toggle), slider(...).on_slide(Msg::Slide), and choice_list(...).on_pick(Msg::Pick). Their messages carry a Boolean, a u16 value, and a stable u32 item ID respectively. Both field and date deliver strings through on_input. Apply an app-selected palette with strata_screen(title).theme(theme).

docs.title: How the games use it
docs.text:
• Falling Blocks binds the Left button to Msg::Move(Move::Left). A left swipe is classified as Move::Left and reaches the same Game::apply_move rule. The game owns its board, score, and phase. The application adapter handles clock ticks, navigation, and saving the high score. Start with samples/falling-blocks/src/view.rs and follow the binding into src/lib.rs.
  • Field Catch binds both keyboard submission and the Join Field button to Msg::JoinField. Its reducer takes an AppInput, which can carry a UI message, a typed WebRTC callback, or another platform event. It returns the next model and effects for the host to execute, such as requesting GPS. Start with samples/field-catch/src/view.rs and follow AppInput and update in src/lib.rs. Navigation and effects

docs.title: Compose the view
docs.text:
A child block accepts immutable let bindings, if let, if/else, match with braced arms, and for. End leaf and component expressions with a semicolon. Return a ViewNode<Msg> for one control or a Fragment<Msg> for several siblings. A fragment adds no native container. Use item-derived keys in loops and give every interactive source a unique key across the whole screen, including toolbar and accessibility actions.

Place header actions in the screen’s toolbar { ... } block. Field Catch enables its video call button when a call is available. The label, availability, and message sit together in the view:

toolbar_item("video-call", "Video call", "video_camera")
    .enabled(can_call)
    .on_press(Msg::VideoCall);

docs.title: How a control becomes a native view
docs.text:
A Control describes what to render. For a map, that includes pins and overlays. A pin can have a glyph, and a circle overlay carries its center, color, and radius in metres. For a button, the control holds its label and optional icon.

A Node places one control in the screen tree and gives it a stable key, styling, and accessibility information. A typed builder such as button(...) lets you bind a Rust message alongside that node. Erosion keeps the binding in Rust and sends the screen description to the phone. When the phone reports a press, the adapter uses the key to find the message.

For a drawing surface, start with canvas(key, width, height), supply the shapes, and bind pointer input with .on_pointer(...). For a map, bind .on_map_idle(...) to remember its viewport or .on_map_heading(...) to follow rotation. Field Catch uses the heading to keep its aiming puck aligned with the map.

docs.title: Keep an editor focused
docs.text:
Give an editable field a key that stays the same as its text changes. The native editor can then keep its focus and selection when Rust renders again. Bind the edit next to the field:

field("title", "Note title", &model.title).on_input(Msg::TitleChanged);
button("save", "Save note").on_press(Msg::Save);

Here Msg::TitleChanged(String) carries the new text into the app. A keyboard submit can send the same Msg::Save as the button. For a list, give each item a persistent ID and use .on_pick(...) to receive it. That way the same item opens after the user sorts or filters the list.

docs.title: Choose an authoring style
docs.text:
Widget functions and chainable modifiers cover common controls. Use Control variants directly for more specialized declarations. The optional ui! macro constructs the same keyed nodes:

use erosion_ui::{ui, widgets::button};
let form = ui!("form" => Column [
    ui!("volume" => Slider { label: "Volume".into(), value: 35 }),
    button("save", "Save"),
]);

The engine compares successive screen descriptions and sends changes over a revisioned bridge. The declarative API, individual widget constructors and both macros use that update path.

docs.title: Draw a custom shape
docs.text:
Build a CanvasPath in the canvas's logical coordinates and put the resulting Draw in the shapes list of Control::Canvas. This leaf has a cubic curve on one side and a quadratic curve on the other.

use erosion_ui::design::CanvasPath;

let leaf = CanvasPath::new(10., 50.)
    .cubic_to(10., 20., 40., 10., 70., 10.)
    .quad_to(65., 50., 10., 50.)
    .close();
let shapes = vec![
    leaf.clone().fill("#568865"),
    leaf.stroke("#294B35", 2.),
];

Curve arguments give the control points first and the endpoint last. Use line_to for straight edges and move_to for another contour. Fills use the nonzero winding rule, so an inner contour drawn in the opposite direction makes a hole. Shapes paint in list order. Stroke widths use canvas units.

docs.title: App-owned native surfaces
docs.text: Field Catch projects its Rust match into a serializable AR scene. It emits a Control::NativeSurface with the renderer name catch-field, a key for the mounted instance, and its scene as JSON properties. The native host creates the view and delivers updated properties on each render. Field Catch implements the renderer in its Android activity and its iOS scene extension. The game owns camera sharing, the ball trajectory, and cleanup when the surface leaves the window.

docs.title: Where a new feature belongs
docs.text:
A new game move, editing command, or validation rule can live entirely in your app’s Rust code. Field Catch adds its own network messages this way. Its map and AR views both read the same match, so switching views preserves the flight in progress.

For an OS feature, first look for an existing device operation. To expose a new capability to every Erosion app, define its request and result in the framework and implement it in the native hosts. For a renderer specific to one app, Field Catch’s AR surface shows how to keep the native implementation alongside the game.

Use the standalone app generator to start another application.

docs.title: Strata starter style
docs.text:
Use strata_screen for Chalk and Basalt. The generated counter and all three samples use this builder. Tap the half-filled circle (the Theme button) in the navigation header to select System, Chalk, or Basalt. System follows the device appearance. Each sample remembers its own choice across launches.

use erosion_ui::widgets::{button, field, strata_screen};

let page = strata_screen("Field note", vec![
    field("title", "Note title", ""),
    button("save", "Save note"),
]);

Chalk pairs a warm paper background with oxide actions. Basalt pairs charcoal green with copper actions. Both use sage for enabled switches, 48-unit minimum button heights, 12-unit button corners, and 16-unit default card corners. Explicit corner radii take precedence. Select Change accent on the Controls Gallery home screen to try the alternate patina accent.

docs.title: Surfaces, corners, and shadows
docs.text:
Import ViewModifiers to style a keyed node. This example groups a native text field and button inside a padded, elevated surface.

use erosion_ui::{
    design::Elevation,
    widgets::{button, column, field, ViewModifiers},
};

let form = column("form", vec![
    field("title", "Title", ""),
    button("save", "Save").rounded(16),
]).surface().padding(16).rounded(20).elevation(Elevation::Medium);

Elevation maps to Android view elevation and UIKit layer shadows. Use Role::Title, Secondary, Accent, and Error to distinguish text by purpose. Pass a theme into the screen builder:

use erosion_ui::widgets::theme;
let palette = theme("#F7F0E4", "#75461E", "#251D19", "#FAC08C");

The arguments are light background, light accent, dark background, and dark accent.

docs.title: Scrolling, wrapping, and rotation
docs.text:
Use column or row for a stack, scroll for a vertically scrollable viewport, and flow to wrap children to available width. For example, flow("actions", 8, buttons) uses a gap of eight logical units between items and lines. A native list handles row reuse.

For structural changes, handle HostEvent::WindowResized { width } and store WidthClass::from_width(width). The wide class starts at 600 dp or points. Gallery’s Layout exhibit switches the same three panels from a column to a row. Its wrap example sets Style::flow_item_width to 88 logical units.

docs.title: Widget motion
docs.text:
Rust declares target values on a stable key. The host animates between targets using the device display clock. In a view! child block, for example:

text("card", "Current score", Role::Accent)
    .scale(if model.expanded { 1.1 } else { 1.0 })
    .rotation(if model.expanded { 3.0 } else { 0.0 })
    .motion(Motion { duration_ms: 180, easing: Easing::EaseOut })
    .feedback(model.score_event, Feedback::Pulse);

Import the motion types from erosion_ui::design and the ViewModifiers trait from erosion_ui::widgets. Translation uses logical units, rotation uses degrees, and scale is uniform about the center.

  • Property change. Set opacity, horizontal or vertical translation, scale, or rotation with a duration and easing. A new widget starts at its declared target.
  • Conditional content. Attach .presence(Presence { enter: Some(PresenceEffect::FadeSlide), exit: Some(PresenceEffect::Fade) }) to the conditional child. Each side can be omitted. Removal immediately drops its input bindings. Eligible visuals finish a 180 ms exit.
  • Layout change. Attach .animate_layout(Motion { duration_ms: 180, easing: Easing::EaseOut }) to a row, column, or flow. Give each child a stable key so it can move and retain focus across reordering. Native scrolling lists handle row movement separately.
  • One-shot feedback. Change the event ID to replay a 240 ms pulse or shake on an existing widget. Keep the ID stable across unrelated renders. Update the score or validation result when the event arrives, independently of animation completion.

Controls Gallery’s Motion & navigation exhibit demonstrates all four. Reduced motion on iOS and disabled animators on Android apply the final state directly.

docs.title: Page transitions
docs.text: Use a navigation transition when an entire page changes. Navigation and effects describes system, fade, and immediate transitions.
